newsitem.title: CHINA: China highway stocks road to reform - World Bank.
newsitem.headline: China highway stocks road to reform - World Bank.

text.p: Recent successful stock issues by Chinese highway firms could provide a model to float other infrastructure projects and fill a gap in China's capital markets, a top World Bank official has said.

China needed to develop a domestic long-term capital market that could tap into its huge domestic savings rate to fund large-scale infrastructure projects, said Pieter Bottelier, chief of the World Bank's mission in Beijing.

The securitisation of existing revenue-earning assets -- such as toll highways -- could pave the way for the issuance of shares and long-term bonds for other projects such as dams, Bottelier told reporters recently.

"Ultimately, China cannot depend on foreign capital for infrastructure development," he said, adding that Beijing should try to limit overseas funds to about 10-15 percent of investment in such projects.

Pension reforms could aid the process by freeing up even more long-term savings that could be sunk into long-term investments, he said, adding that the maturities of almost all bonds now being issued in China were too short to support infrastructure projects.
China is expected to need $65 billion for road construction in the next five years but capital shortfalls are seen at about 15-25 percent of that, the Xinhua news agency said last December.
In the latest move to list by a Chinese toll road operator, Jiangsu Expressway Co Ltd applied last week for a listing on the Hong Kong stock exchange.
That move followed an initial public offering of shares by GZI Transport Ltd, an infrastructure spinoff of Guangzhou Investment Co Ltd, and which was 529 times subscribed.
Sources have said at least six road companies are planning to list on the Hong Kong exchange in 1997.
"This is essentially the privatisation of infrastructure development in China," said Bottelier, whose office has helped to fund Chinese road projects.

If that system takes off, the World Bank may be able to halt its funding for highway projects, he said, adding that the bank had already halted funding for telecommunications as a result of China's rapid development of the sector.
Hydropower projects, with their immense capacity to generate revenue in energy-starved China, could very likely be the next infrastructure candidates to start listing shares, he said.
"The hydropower potential of China is unbelievable," he said.
Bottelier said the new Ertan dam being built on the Yalong River on the border between the southwestern provinces of Sichuan and Yunnan would be perfect for a share float.
"The efficiency of that dam is so great that...it can generate revenue far beyond what it needs to service the loans," he said.
Once the work on the dam was finished, the assets could be securitised and the money raised channelled back into more projects on the river, he said.

China issued one billion yuan ($120 million) in three-year bonds last month to help finance its gargantuan Three Gorges dam project on the Yangtze River. The project's price tag is estimated at 203 billion yuan after adjusting for inflation.

Beijing could also find itself forced to start turning to more commercial financing of infrastructure projects as richer nations became reluctant to give China soft loans through aid agencies, Bottelier said but gave no further details.
